beats.intro: Learning module three. [[sub]]What derivatives do well, what can go wrong, and how issuers and investors use them.
beats.timing: [[line]]Firms often decide something today, but can only transact in the cash market later. [[i1]]A manufacturer orders raw materials before it has customer orders. [[i2]]An importer must pay in a foreign currency when the goods arrive. [[i3]]An issuer wants to lock in the cost of debt it will issue later. [[v1]]An investor has a market view, but not the cash yet. [[v2]]Or knows today how it will reinvest a future coupon. [[bridge]]A derivative bridges that gap. It fixes the price today, for a trade in the future.
beats.montau: [[axes]]Recall Montau, the German exporter. In seventy-five days it will receive six hundred fifty million Korean won, but its costs are in euros. [[exp]]If the won weakens, so that more won are needed per euro, Montau receives fewer euros. Its exposure slopes down. [[fwd]]So Montau sells the won forward at a fixed rate. The forward gains exactly when the won weakens. [[sum]]Add the two together, and the exposure is flat. The currency risk is hedged.
beats.covered: [[long]]Derivatives can also create exposures the cash market cannot. An investor, S C S I, holds a health care stock index and expects it to end the year flat, or slightly higher. [[short]]It sells a call option five percent above today's price, and collects the premium. [[sum]]Together, this is a covered call. If the index rises less than five percent, S C S I keeps its gains plus the premium. [[cap]]Above the exercise price, its upside is capped: the gain is paid away to the option buyer.
beats.discovery: [[head]]Derivative prices also reveal information. This is price discovery. [[d1]]Traders watch stock index futures before the market opens. [[d2]]Interest rate futures show what investors expect a central bank to do. [[d3]]And option prices reveal implied volatility, the market's view of risk. [[oil]]A dramatic case: in April twenty twenty, with demand collapsing and storage full, the expiring oil futures contract closed at minus thirty-seven dollars sixty-three. [[signal]]That signal pushed producers to cut supply faster.
beats.ops: [[head]]Derivatives also have operational advantages. [[o1]]Lower transaction costs: no need to ship, insure or store a commodity. [[o2]]More liquidity, because less capital is needed to trade. [[o3]]Small upfront cash: a margin deposit or a premium, not the full price. [[o4]]And easy short positions, without borrowing the asset. [[eff]]Because mispricing is cheaper to exploit, prices often correct in derivative markets first. Markets become more efficient.
beats.outlay: [[head]]Compare the cash needed for gold. [[spot]]Buying one hundred ounces at the spot price costs one hundred seventy-seven thousand dollars. [[fut]]The futures position needs only the initial margin, four thousand nine hundred fifty dollars. [[int]]Borrowing at five percent for three months, the spot purchase costs two thousand two hundred twelve dollars fifty in interest. [[int2]]The margin costs just sixty-one dollars eighty-eight.
beats.leverage: [[head]]That small outlay means implicit leverage. Gold ends at seventeen eighty fifty. [[spot]]On the spot purchase, the value change is a gain of point five nine three percent. [[fut]]On the futures, the loss of eleven sixty-three, divided by the margin, is minus twenty-three point five percent. [[borrow]]Measured against the borrowing cost alone, the gap is even larger: a forty-seven point five percent gain for spot, against a loss of one thousand eight hundred seventy-nine percent for futures. [[ratio]]Procam controls one hundred seventy-seven thousand dollars of gold for sixty-one dollars eighty-eight of interest: leverage of about two thousand eight hundred sixty. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
beats.risks: [[head]]The main risks of derivatives. [[r1]]Leverage invites speculation, and can lead to financial distress. [[r2]]Complexity can hide the true exposure, as in some structured notes. [[r3]]Basis risk: the derivative may not track the exposure being hedged, for example a different reference rate. [[r4]]Liquidity risk: cash flows arrive at different times, like a margin call before the hedged transaction pays. [[r5]]Counterparty credit risk. [[r6]]And systemic risk: excessive leverage can destabilize markets, as in two thousand eight.
beats.credit: [[call]]Counterparty credit risk depends on the contract. With a purchased call, the buyer depends on the seller to pay at maturity. [[callS]]But once the premium is paid, the seller faces no credit risk from the buyer. [[fwd]]With a forward, either side may end up owed money, so both sides face each other's credit risk. [[mtm]]Daily marking to market on exchanges, and collateral in O T C markets, shrink this risk.
beats.issuer: [[head]]Issuers use derivatives mainly to hedge exposures from their business, to reduce earnings volatility. [[rate]]Back to Montau: the forward rate is thirteen fifty won per euro, so the six hundred fifty million won become four hundred eighty-one thousand four hundred eighty-one euros. The machine costs four hundred thirty thousand euros. [[unh]]Unhedged, the profit margin swings with the exchange rate: from minus one percent to nineteen percent. [[hed]]Hedged, it is eleven percent in every scenario.
beats.accounting: [[head]]Derivatives are reported at fair value, and their gains and losses normally flow through earnings. [[ha]]Hedge accounting lets an issuer match the derivative against the hedged item, to reduce that volatility. There are three designations. [[h1]]A cash flow hedge absorbs variable cash flows, such as a swap from floating to fixed debt, or an F X forward on forecast sales. [[h2]]A fair value hedge offsets changes in the value of an asset or liability, such as swapping fixed-rate debt to floating. [[h3]]A net investment hedge offsets the currency risk of a foreign subsidiary's equity. [[match]]To qualify, the derivative must closely match the hedged item. That is why issuers prefer customized O T C contracts.
beats.investor: [[head]]Investors use derivatives differently. [[u1]]To replicate a cash position cheaply, like Procam's gold futures. [[u2]]To hedge part of a portfolio, such as the currency risk of foreign stocks. [[u3]]And to modify or add exposure: Fyleton's swap added duration, Hightest's call added upside, S C S I's covered call reshaped its payoff. [[nav]]Funds mark derivatives to market every day in their net asset value, so hedge accounting matters less. Investors trade standardized, liquid exchange contracts more often than issuers do.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Derivatives bridge timing gaps and transfer risk, even creating exposures cash markets cannot. [[w2]]They aid price discovery, cut costs and make markets more efficient. [[w3]]Their risks: leverage, complexity, basis, liquidity, counterparty and systemic risk. [[w4]]Issuers hedge with customized contracts and hedge accounting; investors replicate, hedge and modify exposure.
beats.finish: That's the end of learning module three.
